title: On the ultimate nature of reality
subtitle: Graham Harman and Speculative Realism
author: Graham Harman
introduction: Science tells us what things are made of, not what they are. For Graham Harman, Distinguished Professor of Philosophy, named one of the 50 most influential philosophers today, the world’s ultimate nature can’t be captured by equations or unified theories. In his new book Waves and Stones, the leading figure in speculative realism, Graham argues that reality is made of objects that forever withdraw from our grasp, leaving philosophy to explore what science cannot reach. In this exclusive IAI interview, dive into how Graham sees the nature of ultimate reality.
body:
Omari Edwards: Your new book looks at the distinction between Waves and Stones, the continuous and the discrete. What drew you to that as a philosophical problem?

Graham Harman: Sometimes, when I write a book, it is because it is a book I want to read but does not exist yet, so I have to write it myself. This was one of those cases. The distinction between the continuous and the discrete keeps popping up wherever you look, which suggests it is an eminently philosophical problem. And one where too much attention and time has been dedicated to the idea that everything is just in flux, continuous, and objects don't really exist but are just waves in some field.

To explain what I mean: the discrete is the idea that the world is made of detached individual things. The continuous is the idea that the world, or some part of it, is a homogeneous stretch that can be divided however we please. The simplest example is the number line. Between zero and one hundred there are not just one hundred integers. You can count by halves, tenths, or any subdivision at all, so there are infinitely many numbers in that interval. That is what makes a continuum.

Traditionally, space and time have been treated as continua by many philosophers and by contemporary physics in general relativity. They are not made of a definite number of units. You can cut them however you like. Motion is often treated similarly, as an undivided passage from one point to another. By contrast, the discrete is exemplified by individual things, including people. There are two of us in this conversation. That can be counted. What looks like a simple opposition recurs in crucial places across thought and practice.

I want to connect that to your wider project in speculative realism and object-oriented ontology. When you talk about waves and stones, you are not just fitting this distinction into your existing system. You are proposing something new. Before we turn to examples, how does the question connect to object-oriented ontology?

Object-oriented ontology, which I have been working on since my postgraduate studies, talks about the discreteness of objects and what I call their withdrawal, a term I take from Heidegger. Withdrawal means we never have full access to an object. That idea is not unique to me or even to Heidegger. Kant already talks about the thing in itself that we can never reach. We humans are finite and deal with phenomena rather than with noumena.

Reality must be preserved, because without it our statements could never be surprised and we would never change our minds.

What is different in object-oriented ontology is that I do not think this is limited to human thought. It is not that we poor humans cannot reach reality because of our finitude. It is that reality itself never reaches reality the way it really is. You see this in inanimate causation. Consider fire burning cotton, a favourite example in medieval Islamic philosophy and later taken up by Hume. The fire does not interact with every aspect of the cotton. It interacts with the cotton’s flammability, not with its colour or aroma or price. Relations never exhaust their terms. That is a simple philosophical observation.

This is the sense in which things are discrete. Yet they are not completely discrete, otherwise we would have a universe of billions of things that never interact. Some philosophers approached that. Occasionalism in medieval Basra held that God is the only causal agent. It looks like fire burns cotton, but God is making it happen. That position never caught on in medieval Europe, in part because of the problem it poses for free will. Versions of occasionalism reappear later, but I want to avoid any view in which causation is monopolised by a single kind of entity, whether that is God or the human mind. My view is that causation must be explained locally, object by object, despite withdrawal.

Let us go back to Aristotle, who plays a large role in your early chapters. Why bring him in here?

Philosophy does not move as fast as other fields. In many disciplines, if you go back two thousand years, you are in a completely different universe. In philosophy, some very ancient thinkers can still be our contemporaries. When you enter the debate between the continuous and the discrete, there is a human tendency to reduce one to the other. Some say everything is primarily discrete, and continuity is imposed by God or mind. Others say everything is one, continuous flux, and discreteness is secondary.

While working on the book, I saw Aristotle as a thinker who refuses that reduction. Two of his greatest books are the Physics and the Metaphysics. The Physics treats nature and, I argue, the continuous. The Metaphysics treats what we can call the discrete. Aristotle is the philosopher of motion par excellence. He wants to explain how things move.
In the Physics, he discusses number, time, space, and motion as continua that can be divided however we please. He also responds to Zeno’s paradoxes by distinguishing potentiality and actuality. The space between me and a door potentially contains as many points as you like. Actually, moving from here to the door is a single undivided stretch. That is his way of preserving motion without denying the continuum.

In the Metaphysics, Aristotle turns to substances. The world is primarily composed of individual substances. How many people are in this conversation? Two. Not a million. He also treats qualitative change as discrete. Erosion might proceed for a while without noticeable change, then leap. Aristotle thus provides a major precedent for treating the continuous and the discrete as both irreducible.

Readers will also find you positioning philosophy closer to aesthetics than to natural science. How does that apply here?

Since the seventeenth century, natural science has replaced religion as the main authority about reality for many people in the West. Its prestige has led many to try to make what they do into a science, including philosophers. I disagree with that aim. Science is vital, but it is one part of a broader cognitive ecosystem.

Science largely provides knowledge, and there are two basic ways knowledge proceeds. You can tell what a thing is made of, or you can tell what it does. You reduce downward to its pieces, or upward to its effects. Both are important. It matters that water is H2O. It matters that witches are not real and that people misattributed effects. But something is missed in both directions.

I call these undermining, overmining, and their combination duomining. Undermining misses emergence. Hydrogen and oxygen feed fire, while water extinguishes it. Overmining misses what is not currently manifest, which makes it poor at handling counterfactuals. That is why I think philosophy is closer to aesthetics. Aesthetic experience gives a non literal access to the real that cannot be captured by a list of properties. Think of Homer’s phrase, the wine-dark sea. You cannot paraphrase its force into ordinary prose without losing what matters. Metaphor shows how language can touch reality without reducing it to knowledge claims.

How would you respond to the challenge of current analytic philosophies like structural realism, particularly Ladyman and Ross in Everything Must Go. They argue in contrast that all we can ever know is structure and that’s at the basis of reality. What do you think is missing there?

Ladyman and Ross are clear and ambitious. They describe their view as rainforest realism, but for them individual entities end up as correlates of human experience. They accept “Real Patterns” in Dennett’s sense, but those patterns do not have independence from the observer in the way that satisfies me. If the human mind cuts the flux into patterns, the mind must already be distinct from the flux. That is a dualism disguised as monism.

SUGGESTED READING Quantum physics reveals there is no such thing as things By Olimpia Lombardi

For me, objects withdraw not only from humans but from each other. When two objects interact, they do not fully translate each other. There is always loss in translation. Mathematics itself shows this. You cannot project a sphere onto a flat map without distorting areas or shapes. Africa looks smaller than it is on many maps. That is an incommensurability built into representation. Likewise, there is an incommensurability between reality and our knowledge. Every mathematization and every act of equivalence leaves something out. Translation is primordial in any relation.

One chapter of Waves and Stones engages quantum mechanics. Physicists often say quantum theory handles the very small and general relativity the very large. You suggest the deeper bind is between the continuous and the discrete. How so?

Quantum theory and general relativity are incompatible as currently formulated. Quantum theory handles the electromagnetic, strong, and weak forces. General relativity handles gravity. A particle’s position is probabilistic before measurement, yet wherever it is, it curves space-time with its mass. Which space-time does it curve before measurement? That puzzle is one sign of the clash.

The main philosophical difference between me and Žižek, is he is from the German idealist tradition, and he can say as much as he likes that he's not an idealist, but he is.

The small-versus-large rule is a useful shorthand, but not the heart of the problem. You can have quantum effects at macroscopic scales and relativistic effects at very small ones. The real discrepancy is between a continuous curvature of space-time and the discrete behaviour of quanta. That is where the philosophical distinction appears in physics.
There are candidate unifications, such as string theory and loop quantum gravity, but nothing has prevailed. UCL Physicist Jonathan Oppenheim has proposed that general relativity might remain classical, with an interface to quantum theory rather than full reduction. I do not want to tether the book to one proposal, but I do want to suggest that Aristotle’s recognition of both the continuous and the discrete as irreducible might have a place even here.

Many contemporaries, across analytic and continental traditions, use quantum indeterminacy to argue that reality is unstable and self-contradictory and that we should abandon talk of essences. How do you respond, for instance, to Žižek or to Karen Barad?

I know Žižek’s work well, and we disagree here. For him, the human subject is ontologically special, a tear in reality, and contingency is radical. The main philosophical difference between me and Žižek, is he is from the German idealist tradition, and he can say as much as he likes that he's not an idealist, but he is. He often appeals to the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum theory. I have no problem with that interpretation, but I would stress that while position and momentum may be uncertain, the underlying thing that has those properties is not thereby abolished. Properties are entangled with measurement. It does not follow that reality itself is entangled with measurement.

Barad’s influential work develops the notion of intra-action to suggest that what we take as separate entities are parts of one larger process. I think that position risks erasing distinct individuals and their essences. I hold that there are distinct things with their own reality, even if their properties in any specific interaction are entangled with how that interaction occurs.

A central question that recurs while reading you is realism. What does your realism do that a more postmodern scepticism about truth and reality could not do?

The key difference between my view and Kant’s is that Kant does not let us talk about object–object interactions philosophically. The noumenal is a uniquely human cross to bear. In modern philosophy, relations between objects have largely been outsourced to the natural sciences. Ask a typical analytic philosopher to theorise object–object relations and you will often be sent to physics or chemistry. Object-oriented ontology reopens that space.

There will always be mystery. That is not a defect. Negative theology is often mocked for saying only what God is not, but if you read Pseudo-Dionysius you find evocative thinking, not emptiness. His image of one light from three lamps is a memorable way of making the Trinity vivid. Cognition often proceeds by such images. It cannot exhaust a thing with a list of properties.

A plurality of standards is not a weakness but a feature of how collective life works.

On truth and reality, I separate the two. I share some suspicion toward the rhetoric of truth, because it is often used by those who believe they already possess it. I prefer to talk about reality as that which obstructs our expectations and forces decisions. Freud gives a good example when clinical work led him to posit narcissistic libido against his prior assumptions. Reality pushed back. Lacan’s Real is a related notion. Reality must be preserved, because without it our statements could never be surprised and we would never change our minds.

My late friend Bruno Latour held that objects are nothing more than their actions. I argued otherwise, with Aristotle’s criticism of the Megarians in mind. A master builder is still a builder while asleep. Capacities persist off stage. Without that hidden element, nothing could resist or exceed present interactions. That is what the realism is doing. It preserves the autonomy and surprise of things.

As for action, certainty is rare, but decisions are unavoidable. Some matters are compelling enough that we must act without total proof. You can fill in your own examples. The point is that philosophy should help us think clearly about reality’s pressure without pretending to turn philosophy into a lab science.

Let us turn to evolution. You give a sympathetic reading of Stephen Jay Gould and Niles Eldredge on punctuated equilibrium. You claim to not be rejecting science but attending to alternatives. Why foreground Gould rather than, say, Dawkins?

I could have written from Dawkins’s standpoint and reached similar results. His gradualism is largely implicit in a Darwinian framework. Gould and Eldredge explicitly stage the contrast that my book tracks: continuous change versus discrete jumps. They put that tension at the forefront. That is why they belong in a book about waves and stones.

Later I return to Gould in the context of NOMA, the non-overlapping magisteria. Gould, though an agnostic, defended a boundary between science and religion, arguing that each has authority in its own sphere. Dawkins replies that the boundary is porous. If scientific evidence seemed to confirm a religious claim, religious authorities would not stay silent. That exchange is useful for my purposes because it shows how the continuous and the discrete appear as jurisdictional questions too.

You also bring in Latour’s plurality of modes. How does that bear on your realism and on the truth question?

Latour challenges modernity’s tendency to elevate two discourses, scientific and economic, into final arbiters. He decomposes them into multiple modes and shows how other modes constrain them. Law is one clear case. Courts make use of scientific evidence, but judges can exclude it for procedural reasons. Scientific methods do not have the last word in a legal setting. That is widely accepted.

Politics is even more distinct. People sometimes imagine that politics should simply follow the evidence. In reality, politics is where societies decide which evidence counts and to what ends. That does not mean facts do not matter. It means that standards differ across modes. Latour helps us see that a plurality of standards is not a weakness but a feature of how collective life works.

SUGGESTED READING Reality, Closure and the illusion of truth By Hilary Lawson

This becomes painfully clear in situations such as Israel and Palestine. Israel’s current actions in Gaza, for example, clearly violate aspects of international law. If you told that to Prime Minister Netanyahu, he might acknowledge the legal point yet reply that he has a duty to defend his people after October 7, that politics takes precedence over law in an existential crisis. That is when what Carl Schmitt called the “sovereign decision” appears, when a leader claims the right to suspend rules in the name of survival. It is where politics becomes tragic and where philosophy must still analyse without moralizing.

This connects to my realism by resisting both reduction and relativism. We should not reduce law, politics, or religion to science. Nor should we deny that there is a reality that pushes back within each mode. The continuous and the discrete remain active at these boundaries.

Earlier, you discussed the dialectic of civilisation and barbarism through Ibn Khaldun, Kublai Khan, and Timur. Could you restate that briefly as we close?

Ibn Khaldun offers two relevant ideas. First, generations decline. Civilizations grow decadent and are replaced by outsiders. Second, he distinguishes nomadic from civilized peoples. Nomads often sack cities, yet over time they are tempted by urban luxuries and settle. Kublai Khan exemplifies that trajectory. Within a few generations of ferocious conquest, he becomes emperor of China, adopts administrative refinements, and hosts learned debates. That is the barbarian becoming civilized.

There is also a reverse movement that Ibn Khaldun does not thematize, where the civilized are tempted by barbarism. Timur shows that, as do many episodes in state history. The deeper reason is fear. The more you have, the more you fear losing it. That fear can produce atrocities in the name of preservation. It is a reminder that our categories are not fixed. The continuous pressure of circumstance and the discrete decisions of leaders interact, often tragically.

Before we finish, any final word you want to add in a more positive light, and perhaps a practical note for readers?

Yes. There is an audiobook. For the first time I read my own work in the studio. It gave me new respect for voice actors. It may not release on the exact date of the hardcover, but it will follow shortly for anyone who prefers to listen.

Thanks for joining us.

Thank you.

You can pick up your own copy of Waves and Stones now at all good book stores.
